careers.name: UX Designer
careers.description: Make everyday digital experiences simpler, more useful, and more human.
careers.reality: Expect revisions, detailed documentation, and balancing user needs with business constraints.
careers.aiNote: AI can speed up drafts and mockups. Understanding people and judging what is worth building stays human.
careers.project: redesign one screen of an app you use every day

scenes.title: A real problem. Your approach.
scenes.prompt: Your team is building a campus wellbeing app. Students keep abandoning the booking screen, but the team wants to add more features. What would you do first?

choices.text: Create a fresh design right away
choices.outcome: The team has something polished by lunch. Testing shows students still leave at the same step, and someone asks what evidence guided the redesign.

choices.text: Talk to students before changing the design
choices.outcome: Three short conversations reveal that students don’t trust the screen to confirm their booking. You now have a specific problem to solve, though it cost you part of the morning.

choices.text: Study existing usage patterns first
choices.outcome: Analytics show where people leave, but not why. You have a useful clue and a new question to take to students.

scenes.title: The next choice matters.
scenes.prompt: A student says the booking screen feels overwhelming. Your deadline is tomorrow. How do you decide what to change?

choices.text: Explain the trade-offs and agree on one priority
choices.outcome: The team agrees on one change. It’s a clear plan, though you haven’t yet tested whether it fixes the student’s problem.

choices.text: Add every improvement the team requested
choices.outcome: Everything ships on time, but the screen is busier than before. The deadline gets tight and nobody is sure which change helped.

choices.text: Test one simpler version with a few students
choices.outcome: Four students try the simpler version and finish booking without help. You leave with evidence, a smaller scope, and a team that trusts the decision.

careers.name: Data Analyst
careers.description: Turn messy information into clear insights that help people make decisions.
careers.reality: A lot of time goes into cleaning data, checking assumptions, and explaining uncertainty.
careers.aiNote: AI can write queries and charts quickly. Asking the right question and spotting bad data still needs a person.
careers.project: analyse a small public dataset and share three findings

scenes.title: A real problem. Your approach.
scenes.prompt: You’re analysing a campus survey. One chart suggests a big increase in stress, but a quarter of the responses are incomplete. The team needs your report today. What would you do?

choices.text: Share the most exciting pattern immediately
choices.outcome: The headline spreads fast. Then a colleague points out the missing responses and you have to issue a correction.

choices.text: Ask the team which question matters most
choices.outcome: The team narrows the question, which saves time. You still need to check the data quality before anything is shared.

choices.text: Check missing values and verify the source
choices.outcome: The incomplete responses all came from one department. After adjusting, the increase is real but smaller. The report is later than hoped, and it holds up.

scenes.title: The next choice matters.
scenes.prompt: After checking the survey, the trend is smaller than expected. Your manager prefers the dramatic headline. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Show both interpretations with clear caveats
choices.outcome: Your manager sees the options, but the caveats get lost in the summary. You’ll need to make the uncertainty easier to read.

choices.text: Present the verified finding and its limitations
choices.outcome: It’s a less dramatic story, but it survives questions. Your manager asks you to present it to the wider team.

choices.text: Use the bigger number to get attention
choices.outcome: The number gets attention, then scrutiny. When someone reruns the analysis, trust in your reports drops.

careers.name: Environmental Scientist
careers.description: Investigate our natural world and help communities protect its future.
careers.reality: Fieldwork, technical reports, and slow-moving policy decisions are part of the work.
careers.aiNote: AI can help analyse sensor and satellite data. Fieldwork and community trust still depend on people.
careers.project: track one local environmental measure for two weeks

scenes.title: A real problem. Your approach.
scenes.prompt: You’re helping investigate water quality near a community garden. A single sample looks unusual, but the other results are normal. Residents want an answer today. How would you respond?

choices.text: Tell residents all is fine because most samples are normal
choices.outcome: Residents are relieved, until a colleague notices the unusual sample you left out. You have to walk the message back.

choices.text: Report a possible risk with clear uncertainty
choices.outcome: Residents appreciate the honesty, though some worry more than necessary. You’ll need to explain what “possible” means.

choices.text: Collect more samples before drawing conclusions
choices.outcome: A second round takes a day, but the picture gets clearer. You can tell residents what you know and when you’ll know more.

scenes.title: The next choice matters.
scenes.prompt: A second sample suggests a possible issue. A sponsor asks you to keep the result quiet until next month. What do you do?

choices.text: Explain uncertainty and seek an independent review
choices.outcome: An outside reviewer agrees the result needs follow-up. It’s the right direction, though reporting steps still need to be followed.

choices.text: Wait quietly to avoid upsetting the sponsor
choices.outcome: The sponsor is pleased for now. Weeks later the delay becomes the story, and people question your independence.

choices.text: Document findings and follow reporting procedures
choices.outcome: Your records are clear and the right people are informed on time. The sponsor is unhappy, but nobody can question your process.

careers.name: Software Engineer
careers.description: Design, build, and improve the software people rely on every day.
careers.reality: Debugging, code reviews, and unclear requirements take up as much time as building new things.
careers.aiNote: AI can draft code. Engineers still decide what to build, check it works, and take responsibility for it.
careers.skill: one programming language such as Python or JavaScript
careers.project: build a small tool that solves a problem you have

scenes.title: Something just broke.
scenes.prompt: A student-built booking app crashes for some users after your latest release. Reports are coming in. What do you do first?

choices.text: Start fixing the bug directly in production
choices.outcome: You find the cause quickly, but your patch introduces a second bug while users are still affected.

choices.text: Roll back the release, then investigate calmly
choices.outcome: Users recover within minutes. In a safe environment you reproduce the crash and find a missing check for an empty field.

choices.text: Ask users for screenshots before changing anything
choices.outcome: The screenshots help narrow things down, but the crashes continue while you wait.

scenes.title: The next choice matters.
scenes.prompt: A teammate wants to ship an exciting new feature today. It’s untested, and the deadline is tomorrow. What do you suggest?

choices.text: Delay the whole feature until everything is perfect
choices.outcome: Nothing breaks, but the team misses the chance to learn from real users and the deadline slips.

choices.text: Add tests for the riskiest parts, then ship a smaller version
choices.outcome: You ship a smaller version that works. Two small issues are caught by tests before users ever see them.

choices.text: Ship it today and fix problems as they appear
choices.outcome: The feature launches, and so do three bugs. You spend the evening patching instead of improving.

careers.name: Teacher
careers.description: Help learners understand new ideas and grow in confidence.
tasks: Support students and talk with families
careers.reality: Marking, planning, and managing a busy classroom happen alongside the moments that make it worthwhile.
careers.aiNote: AI can help prepare materials. Noticing who needs help and building trust in a classroom stays human.
careers.project: teach a friend one topic in 10 minutes and ask what was unclear

scenes.title: A class that’s drifting.
scenes.prompt: Halfway through a lesson, several students look lost while others look bored. What do you do?

choices.text: Keep going to finish the planned lesson
choices.outcome: You finish on time, but the next quiz shows the same gaps, and a few students have stopped trying.

choices.text: Slow down and re-explain everything to the whole class
choices.outcome: The confused students catch up, but the others lose focus. You’ll want a better way to pace for different needs.

choices.text: Pause and ask a quick question to see who understands what
choices.outcome: A two-minute check shows two different gaps. You split the class briefly and both groups re-engage.

scenes.title: A message from home.
scenes.prompt: A capable student has stopped handing in work. A parent emails asking why their grade has dropped.

choices.text: Talk to the student privately first, then reply to the parent
choices.outcome: The student admits things are hard at home. You reply to the parent with specifics and a plan, and the student feels heard.

choices.text: Send a firm reply citing the grade policy
choices.outcome: The reply is accurate but cold. The parent escalates, and the student still hasn’t been asked what’s going on.

choices.text: Ask a colleague what they have noticed
choices.outcome: Your colleague has seen the same pattern. It’s useful context, but you still need to talk to the student.

careers.name: Nurse
careers.description: Care for patients, watch for risks, and support people on difficult days.
careers.reality: Shifts are long and emotionally demanding, and mistakes carry real consequences. Careful routines matter.
careers.aiNote: AI can help with records and alerts. Hands-on care and human judgement at the bedside stay central.
careers.project: shadow or interview a nurse about a typical shift

scenes.title: A detail that doesn’t match.
scenes.prompt: During handover you notice a patient’s notes list an allergy, but their wristband doesn’t show it. What do you do?

choices.text: Ask the previous nurse to fix it when she’s next in
choices.outcome: The issue gets fixed, but hours later. In the meantime, patient safety depends on someone else’s schedule.

choices.text: Assume the notes are right and carry on with your round
choices.outcome: Nothing goes wrong this time. A colleague later points out how close the gap came to causing harm.

choices.text: Verify with the patient and chart, then update the wristband and tell the team
choices.outcome: The allergy is real, and the wristband is corrected before the next medication round. The few extra minutes prevented a real risk.

scenes.title: An upset family member.
scenes.prompt: A patient’s family member is upset about a delay and wants to speak to someone in charge. You have three other tasks waiting.

choices.text: Tell them you’re too busy to talk right now
choices.outcome: The family member feels dismissed and raises their voice. You lose more time calming things down than a short conversation would have taken.

choices.text: Listen first, explain what you know, and offer to bring the charge nurse
choices.outcome: Two calm minutes help the family feel informed. The charge nurse follows up, and your other tasks are only briefly delayed.

choices.text: Pass them straight to the charge nurse
choices.outcome: The concern is escalated correctly, but the family member feels brushed off in the moment.

careers.name: Product Manager
careers.description: Decide what to build next by listening to users and balancing what a team can deliver.
tasks: Talk to users and gather feedback
careers.reality: You’re often responsible for outcomes without direct authority, and you’ll say no to good ideas regularly.
careers.aiNote: AI can summarise feedback and draft specs. Weighing trade-offs and aligning people remains your job.
careers.skill: prioritising with a simple impact and effort grid
careers.project: run a tiny survey and decide what to improve first

scenes.title: Three teams, one slot.
scenes.prompt: Three teams want their feature on this month’s plan, but you can only fit one. How do you decide?

choices.text: Pick the loudest team’s request to keep the peace
choices.outcome: It’s quiet for a week. Then the other teams ask why they weren’t heard, and nobody can explain your reasoning.

choices.text: Compare each against user impact and effort, then explain your choice
choices.outcome: One feature clearly helps the most users for the least effort. Two teams are disappointed, but they understand why.

choices.text: Ask each team to present, then vote
choices.outcome: Everyone feels heard, but the vote favours the best presenter rather than the best idea.

scenes.title: A launch that isn’t landing.
scenes.prompt: Early data shows a feature you launched isn’t being used. The team is proud of it. What happens next?

choices.text: Remove it right away to save maintenance time
choices.outcome: It saves effort, but you haven’t learned why people ignored it, so the next feature might repeat the problem.

choices.text: Interview a few users to understand why before deciding
choices.outcome: Users say they never found it. A small change to where it appears doubles usage within a week.

choices.text: Promote it harder and hope people notice
choices.outcome: Clicks go up briefly, but people still don’t use it. The team spent energy without learning anything.

careers.name: Journalist
careers.description: Find out what’s happening, check it carefully, and tell stories people need to hear.
careers.reality: Tight deadlines, uncertain pay in many outlets, and pressure from people who’d rather a story not run.
careers.aiNote: AI can transcribe and summarise. Verifying facts and earning a source’s trust are human work.
careers.project: write a 300-word story about something in your community

scenes.title: A tip with one source.
scenes.prompt: An anonymous message says a local business is dumping waste. It’s your only source, and your editor wants a story by evening.

choices.text: Ask the business for comment first, then decide
choices.outcome: The business denies it quickly. You’ve learned their position, but you still have no independent evidence either way.

choices.text: Look for a second independent source and public records before writing
choices.outcome: Council records show two earlier complaints. You have enough to write a careful story, though it may miss the evening deadline.

choices.text: Publish it as a “reported claim” to beat other outlets
choices.outcome: You’re first, but with nothing to back it up. The business’s lawyer calls within the hour.

scenes.title: A source gets nervous.
scenes.prompt: A source you trust asks to take back what they told you, saying they’re nervous about the consequences.

choices.text: Use the quote anyway because they did say it
choices.outcome: You break the source’s trust. They stop talking to you, and other potential sources hear about it.

choices.text: Talk through their concerns and what’s on the record, respecting agreed terms
choices.outcome: They agree to speak on background. You keep the information, your word, and a source who will talk to you again.

choices.text: Drop the story completely
choices.outcome: You avoid the conflict, but a story the public needed goes untold, and you haven’t tried to find a safer way.

dna_scenarios.title: The Unfamiliar City
narrative: You have just arrived in a city you have never visited before. You need to reach a meeting point across town within 90 minutes. You have a paper map, a written set of directions from a local, and you can see a tall landmark tower in the distance. Your phone has died.

options.text: Study the paper map, mentally rotating it to align with your current orientation, and plot a route using the landmark tower as a reference point.
Read through the written directions carefully, memorizing the sequence of street names and turns described.
Approach a group of people nearby and ask them to walk you through the best route, reading their body language to judge how confident they are in their directions.
Start walking toward the landmark tower, reasoning that if you maintain a consistent direction and track the logical grid pattern of streets, you will converge on the destination.
Look around for environmental patterns—notice which direction foot traffic flows, where commercial activity clusters, and infer the city center's location from these cues.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Research confirms that spatial ability is separable from general ability factors (Skarzyński & Noworol, 2022), and that field independence contributes independently to problem-solving. The map-rotation option (A) directly taps mental rotation and spatial visualization—capacities measured by instruments like the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test (Gimena et al., 2015). Option C assesses interpersonal intelligence, which Gardner defines as the ability to understand and interact effectively with others Zainudin et al. (2024). The branching logic proceeds based on the user's dominant response pattern.

dna_scenarios.title: Spatial Dominant Path
narrative: You orient the map successfully and begin walking. After 15 minutes, you reach a complex intersection where five streets converge at odd angles. The map shows this intersection but the scale makes it difficult to determine which street is which. Three of the streets look nearly identical from where you stand.
dna_scenarios.prompt: How do you determine which street to take?

options.text: Mentally reconstruct a three-dimensional model of the intersection from the two-dimensional map, comparing angles between streets on the map to what you see.
Walk a short distance down each candidate street, checking whether the buildings and features match what the map predicts should appear next.
Count the streets clockwise from the direction you arrived and match that to the map's orientation.

dna_scenarios.rationale: This branch deepens spatial assessment. Research using the Object-Spatial Imagery and Verbal Questionnaire (OSIVQ) distinguishes between object imagery (pictorial appearances) and spatial imagery (spatial relations and transformations) (Almufareh & Almaleh, 2026; . Response A1 taps spatial visualization specifically—"schematic images, spatial relations amongst objects and spatial transformations" (Almufareh & Almaleh, 2026; —while A2 introduces bodily-kinesthetic exploration.

dna_scenarios.title: Social Intelligence Dominant Path
narrative: The group you approached includes three people. One gives you confident, detailed directions while making steady eye contact. Another interrupts with a contradictory route, speaking quickly and gesturing vaguely. The third person stays quiet but subtly shakes their head when the second person speaks.

options.text: Follow the first person's directions because their confident demeanor and eye contact suggest familiarity with the area.
Ask the quiet third person directly what they think, since their subtle head-shake suggests they have knowledge but are socially deferring to the louder speaker.
Ask all three to reach a consensus before you proceed, facilitating a brief discussion.
Ignore the social dynamics entirely and ask each person to point in the direction of a well-known landmark to triangulate the correct route.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Interpersonal intelligence encompasses understanding others' motivations and feelings, while intrapersonal intelligence involves understanding one's own Zainudin et al. (2024). Response C2 demonstrates advanced social perception—reading non-verbal micro-cues and understanding social hierarchies within groups. Research on prosocial traits shows that object-oriented imagery is associated with empathy and the ability to be transported into others' perspectives (Song et al., 2026). This scenario assesses whether the user reads implicit social information (C2), relies on explicit social signals (C1), or defaults to non-social problem-solving (C4).

dna_scenarios.title: The Data Puzzle
narrative: You are given a temporary job at the meeting point. Your task: a company has sales data from six regions over twelve months. The data is presented in three formats simultaneously—a spreadsheet of numbers, a set of colored bar charts, and a written narrative summary. You have 20 minutes to identify which region is underperforming and why.

options.text: Go straight to the spreadsheet, calculate percentage changes month-over-month, and look for statistical anomalies.
Scan the bar charts first, looking for visual patterns—dips, trends, color-coded outliers—before checking numbers.
Read the narrative summary first to understand the context, then verify claims against the data.
Compare all three formats simultaneously, cross-referencing to find inconsistencies between them.
Ask a colleague who has worked with this data before what they think, then verify their intuition against the evidence.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Intelligence reflects "a broad capability for comprehending our surroundings, solving problems, planning, or learning from experience" (Shen et al., 2026). The Differential Aptitude Test measures multiple subtests defining a cognitive profile, based on the premise that human intelligence comprises many different levels of proficiency (Srianturi & Supriatna, 2020). Response D, which integrates multiple information modalities, reflects the highest general cognitive ability as it requires simultaneous processing across representational systems. Research on cognitive styles confirms that visualizers favor pictorial and spatial representations while verbalizers prefer linguistic formats (Akos et al., 2004), making format preference a reliable indicator of cognitive style.

dna_scenarios.title: Logical-Mathematical Deep Dive
narrative: You discover that Region 4 shows a 23% decline in Q3. The spreadsheet reveals that three product categories dropped simultaneously. However, Region 4's customer count actually increased by 8% during the same period.

options.text: The average transaction value decreased—more customers buying less per visit—suggesting a pricing or product mix problem.
There may be a data entry error, since increasing customers and decreasing sales is unusual enough to warrant verification.
A competitor entered the market in Q3, capturing the higher-value customers while Region 4 retained only lower-spending ones.
Seasonal factors specific to Region 4's geography may explain the pattern—you look for whether this happened in previous years.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Fluid intelligence—the ability to perceive relationships independent of prior learning—is assessed through novel problem-solving Coertse & Schepers, 2004). Response A1 demonstrates deductive reasoning from available data. Response A3 introduces creative hypothesis generation, reflecting practical and creative intelligence necessary for career success Zainudin et al. (2024). Response A4 demonstrates pattern recognition across temporal contexts, tapping naturalistic intelligence (recognizing patterns in complex systems).

dna_scenarios.title: The Design Challenge
narrative: Your next task requires you to redesign the layout of a small retail space. You are given the room dimensions (8m × 12m), the inventory of display units (varying sizes), and the constraint that customers must be able to reach any product within 30 seconds of entering. You also know that 60% of customers are right-handed and tend to turn right upon entering.

options.text: Sketch a bird's-eye floor plan to scale, placing units and mentally simulating customer flow paths.
Build a mathematical model: calculate the maximum distance from the entrance to any point, then optimize unit placement to minimize average path length.
Think about how you personally feel when entering retail spaces—what makes you comfortable, what frustrates you—and design from that emotional intuition.
Research how successful retail spaces are designed, looking for established principles and best practices to apply.
Imagine yourself as different types of customers—elderly, hurried, browsing—and mentally walk through the space from each perspective.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Spatial visualization—"the ability to perceive relationships independent of prior learning" in spatial contexts Coertse & Schepers, 2004)—is directly assessed by option A. Research demonstrates that spatial imagery tendencies are stronger among students in sciences and engineering, with Physics Engineering students scoring highest (M=3.81) on spatial imagery scales (Steppan et al., 2026). Option E taps perspective-taking, a core component of interpersonal intelligence associated with empathy (Song et al., 2026).

dna_scenarios.title: The Conflict
narrative: You are placed on a team of five to complete a project. During the first meeting, two team members immediately clash. Person X presents a detailed, data-driven plan and dismisses alternatives. Person Y advocates for a creative, unconventional approach and becomes visibly frustrated when X ignores their ideas. The other two members stay silent, looking uncomfortable. The deadline is in three days.

options.text: Analyze both proposals objectively, identify the strengths of each, and present a merged plan that incorporates the best elements.
Address the emotional tension directly: acknowledge that both X and Y feel strongly, validate their perspectives, and facilitate a structured discussion where each person speaks uninterrupted.
Take charge and assign specific tasks to each person based on what you perceive their strengths to be, bypassing the conflict entirely.
Privately approach the two silent members to understand their views, then use that information to build a coalition for the best approach.
Step back and observe the dynamics for a while longer before intervening, trying to understand the underlying motivations driving each person's behavior.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Holland's RIASEC model identifies the Social and Enterprising dimensions as critical career-relevant constructs (Mrabet & Moussa, 2021). Personality and interest are determinants of career achievement within congruent environments (Mrabet & Moussa, 2021). Career maturity research shows that personality constructs—not cognitive constructs alone—differentiate career-mature from career-immature individuals (Tuccio et al., 2023), making social-emotional assessment essential. Response B demonstrates the highest interpersonal intelligence through explicit emotional validation and structured facilitation. Response E reflects intrapersonal intelligence—understanding one's own reactions and exercising metacognitive restraint.

dna_scenarios.title: High Social Intelligence Path
narrative: You successfully facilitate the discussion. Person X softens and shares that they are anxious about the deadline because a previous project failure cost them a promotion. Person Y reveals they feel chronically undervalued in team settings. The two silent members now engage—one has a technical background and the other has client-facing experience.
dna_scenarios.prompt: How do you structure the remaining work?

options.text: Assign X to quality control and timeline management (leveraging their anxiety as vigilance), Y to ideation and creative direction (channeling their need for recognition), the technical member to implementation, and the client-facing member to presentation.
Create pairs: X with the client-facing member (to balance X's rigidity with interpersonal skill) and Y with the technical member (to ground Y's creativity in feasibility). You coordinate.
Let the team self-organize now that tensions are resolved, offering to help wherever needed.
Propose that everyone works on every component together, rotating roles to build mutual understanding.

dna_scenarios.rationale: This branch assesses advanced social intelligence—the ability to translate interpersonal understanding into strategic action. Response B1 demonstrates the highest integration of psychological insight with organizational logic, converting emotional vulnerabilities into functional strengths. This aligns with the MDPA algorithm's approach of matching personality profiles to optimal roles through "non-linear threshold penalties for critical traits" Banai & Perin (2016).

dna_scenarios.title: The Ethical Dilemma
narrative: During the project, you discover that the data your team is using contains a significant error that, if corrected, would make your team's conclusions less impressive. The client will likely never notice the error. Correcting it means missing the deadline. Your team members are divided—two want to ignore it, one wants to correct it, and one defers to you.

options.text: Correct the error immediately, inform the client about the delay, and explain why accuracy matters more than speed.
Quantify the impact of the error—if it changes the conclusion by less than 5%, proceed; if more, correct it.
Present both the corrected and uncorrected findings to the client, letting them decide which version to use.
Correct the error but find a way to compress other work to still meet the deadline, even if it means working through the night.
Consult with the team member who wants to correct it to understand their reasoning, then make a collective decision.

dna_scenarios.title: The Unfamiliar System
narrative: You are given access to a software tool you have never used before. It has no tutorial. The interface has icons, menus, and a command line. You need to produce a specific output (a formatted report) within 45 minutes.

options.text: Systematically click through every menu and icon, building a mental map of the software's structure before attempting the task.
Look for a "Help" or documentation section and read it thoroughly before touching anything.
Try to produce the report immediately through trial and error, learning from each mistake.
Look for patterns between this software and others you have used, applying familiar conventions (e.g., Ctrl+S to save, File menu for export).
Search for the command line syntax by typing "help" or "?" and work from text-based instructions.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Learning ability assessment requires observing how individuals approach novel problems. Crystallized intelligence draws on "knowledge from prior learning and experience" (option D), while fluid intelligence involves "the ability to perceive relationships independent of prior learning" (option C) Coertse & Schepers, 2004). The Learning Speed score reflects career adaptability—"combining planning, control, exploration, and confidence" Sarsenbay et al. (2026)—which bridges AI acceptance and employability.

dna_scenarios.title: The Feedback Loop
narrative: You tried several approaches. Your first attempt produced a garbled output. Your second attempt produced a partially correct report but with wrong formatting. On your third attempt, you noticed that the formatting toolbar only appears after selecting text.
dna_scenarios.prompt: What did you learn from this sequence?

options.text: The software uses context-sensitive menus—tools appear only when relevant objects are selected. You now predict that chart-editing tools will appear only when a chart is selected.
You need to slow down and read the interface more carefully before clicking.
The software is poorly designed and you would prefer a different tool.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Response C-i demonstrates the highest learning ability—extracting a generalizable principle from specific experiences and predicting its application in a novel context. This mirrors the TTT-GP-CGS methodology where "if the student's score increases day by day, it reflects that the student has good learning ability" Lubinski (2004). The system tracks not just what the user chose but whether they can articulate transferable learning.

dna_scenarios.title: The Composition
narrative: You are asked to create a short presentation that will move an audience emotionally. The topic is "the passage of time." You have access to images, music, text, physical props, and video. You have 30 minutes to prepare a 3-minute presentation.
dna_scenarios.prompt: What is the centerpiece of your presentation?

options.text: A carefully sequenced series of photographs showing the same location across decades, with no narration—letting the visual progression speak for itself.
A piece of music that shifts tempo and key, paired with a single slowly changing image.
A spoken narrative—a personal story about a moment when you became aware of time passing—delivered with deliberate pacing and pauses.
A physical demonstration: you bring a candle, light it at the start, and let it burn down during your presentation while you speak minimally.
A philosophical question posed to the audience: "If you could relive one hour of your life, which would it be and why?"—then silence, letting them reflect.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Gardner's multiple intelligences framework includes musical, bodily-kinesthetic, and existential dimensions Banai & Perin (2016). Research on cognitive styles confirms that visual cognitive style was more important than verbal cognitive style for assessing creative products among art and design students (Jammalamadaka, 2019). This scenario simultaneously assesses creative intelligence and dominant modality preference.

dna_scenarios.title: The Physical Challenge
narrative: You need to learn a new physical skill: assembling a complex piece of flat-pack furniture with 47 parts and an instruction booklet with diagrams but no text. The diagrams are small and somewhat ambiguous.

options.text: Lay out all 47 parts, sort them by type and size, and match each to its diagram before beginning assembly.
Start assembling immediately, using the diagrams as rough guides and relying on how the pieces physically feel and fit together.
Study the final product image and work backward, reasoning about which structural elements must be assembled first.
Search online for a video tutorial of someone assembling the same item.
Call a friend who is good at this sort of thing and assemble it together.

dna_scenarios.title: The Career Crossroads
narrative: You receive two job offers simultaneously. Job A pays 40% more, is in a field you find intellectually stimulating, but requires relocating to a city where you know no one. Job B pays less, is in a field you find moderately interesting, but is near family and friends and offers strong mentorship.
dna_scenarios.prompt: What is the FIRST thing you think about?

options.text: You create a spreadsheet comparing salary, cost of living, career growth projections, and long-term financial outcomes.
You imagine yourself in each scenario six months from now—what does your daily life look and feel like?
You call three people you trust and ask for their perspectives before forming your own opinion.
You reflect on what has made you happiest in past jobs and whether either offer aligns with those patterns.
You research both companies' trajectories, industry trends, and which field is more likely to grow over the next decade.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Career decision-making requires both cognitive and affective maturity (Orzan, 2026). Social Cognitive Career Theory emphasizes that self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and personal interests jointly shape career decisions (Tountopoulou et al., 2021). Response D demonstrates the highest intrapersonal intelligence—the capacity for self-knowledge that career readiness research identifies as a critical developmental need, with 8th-grade students showing "developmentally appropriate elevated needs for information, specifically self-knowledge" (Memari & Ruggles, 2025). Computational psychometrics advocates for navigation components including "self-knowledge of abilities and interests, knowledge about academic major and occupations, and skills related to planning and decision-making" (Davis, 2021).

dna_scenarios.title: The Failure
narrative: You invested significant effort into a project that ultimately failed. Your approach was sound, your execution was diligent, but external factors beyond your control caused the failure. A colleague who invested less effort succeeded due to favorable circumstances.
dna_scenarios.prompt: What is your dominant internal response?

options.text: You analyze exactly what external factors caused the failure and whether you could have anticipated them—extracting lessons for next time.
You feel frustrated but recognize that the frustration is about fairness, not competence—you separate your self-worth from the outcome.
You talk to the successful colleague to understand what they did differently, genuinely curious rather than resentful.
You feel motivated to try again immediately, viewing the failure as a data point rather than a verdict.
You reflect on whether this type of work truly aligns with your values, or whether the failure is a signal to redirect your energy.

dna_scenarios.rationale: Career adaptability—combining planning, control, exploration, and confidence—serves as a psychological resource for navigating career changes Sarsenbay et al. (2026). Hope for success is a demonstrated predictor of career path choices among vocational students (Satterly, 1976). Response D reflects the highest career adaptability, while Response B demonstrates advanced emotional self-regulation, a component of intrapersonal intelligence.

dna_scenarios.title: The System
narrative: You are managing a greenhouse with four types of plants. You observe the following over two weeks:
• When Plant A is watered daily, Plant B (in the adjacent bed) grows faster, but Plant C (two beds away) wilts.
• When Plant A is watered every other day, all plants grow at normal rates.
• Plant D only flowers when Plant C is healthy.
• The greenhouse needs all four plants flowering simultaneously for a client visit in 10 days.

options.text: Water Plant A every other day for the first 7 days (keeping C healthy so D flowers), then switch to daily watering for the last 3 days to boost B's growth, accepting that C may wilt slightly but D has already flowered.
Water Plant A daily but move Plant C farther away from A to test whether proximity is the causal factor.
Water Plant A every other day throughout, accepting slower growth for B but ensuring C and D remain healthy.
Create a mathematical model of the relationships: A→B (positive, proximity-dependent), A→C (negative, distance-dependent), C→D (conditional), and optimize the watering schedule.

dna_scenarios.rationale: This scenario assesses fluid intelligence—reasoning about novel relational systems without prior training Coertse & Schepers, 2004). Response A demonstrates the highest integration of temporal planning with causal reasoning. Response B demonstrates scientific thinking (hypothesis testing through controlled manipulation). The NADINE assessment framework similarly measures "decision making, problem solving... cognitive/analytical skills" through performance-based tasks Coertse & Schepers, 2004).

logical.label: Logical-Mathematical
logical.blurb: I reason step by step and trust evidence and structure.

spatial.label: Spatial-Visual
spatial.blurb: I think in shapes, maps and mental pictures.

verbal.label: Verbal-Linguistic
verbal.blurb: I think best through words, explanations and stories.

inter.label: Interpersonal
inter.blurb: I read people well and do my best work with others.

intra.label: Intrapersonal
intra.blurb: I know my own motives and reflect before I act.

bodily.label: Bodily-Kinesthetic
bodily.blurb: I learn by doing, moving and handling things.

musical.label: Musical
musical.blurb: I notice rhythm, sound and pattern over time.

naturalistic.label: Naturalistic
naturalistic.blurb: I spot patterns in living and complex systems.

existential.label: Existential
existential.blurb: I keep asking why, about meaning and purpose.

fluid.label: Fluid Intelligence
fluid.blurb: I work out brand-new problems without a rulebook.

learning.label: Learning Ability
learning.blurb: I pick up new systems fast and transfer what I learn.

adapt.label: Career Adaptability
adapt.blurb: I plan, explore and bounce back when things change.

creative.label: Creative Intelligence
creative.blurb: I generate original ideas and unexpected angles.
